summary: This note summarizes the linguistic landscape of India, drawing on the 2001 Census of India, which counted 122 major languages and 1599 other languages while noting that counts vary by source due to differing definitions of language and dialect. It describes the historical roles of Persian and English as contact languages, the spread of Hindi as a lingua franca and the resulting anti-Hindi agitations, and the constitutional recognition of 22 scheduled languages and six classical languages.
one_line: Overview of India's languages, census counts, the historical roles of Persian and English, Hindi's status, and scheduled and classical language recognition.
key_facts: The Census of India of 2001 counted 122 major languages and 1599 other languages in India.
Figures for the number of languages in India vary across sources, primarily due to differences in the definition of the terms 'language' and 'dialect'.
The 2001 Census recorded 30 languages spoken by more than a million native speakers.
The 2001 Census recorded 122 languages spoken by more than 10,000 people.
Persian was the court language during the Mughal period in India.
Persian reigned as an administrative language for several centuries until the era of British colonisation.
English continues to be an important language in India and is used in higher education and in some areas of the Indian government.
Hindi is the most widely spoken language in a large region of India and serves as the lingua franca across much of North and Central India.
There have been anti-Hindi agitations in South India, most notably in the state of Tamil Nadu.
There is opposition in non-Hindi belt states towards the imposition of Hindi in these areas.
The Eighth Schedule of the Indian Constitution lists 22 languages, referred to as scheduled languages.
The Government of India has awarded classical language status to Kannada, Malayalam, Odia, Sanskrit, Tamil and Telugu.
Classical language status is given to languages which have a rich heritage and independent nature.
